meta.label: Password managers
meta.attribution: Curated from public security audits, open-source status, and breach history - not measured data. A password manager is still far safer than reusing passwords; this helps you pick a trustworthy one. Verify current details yourself. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare password managers by security, everyday access, privacy, and disclosure.

axes.label: Privacy
axes.question: Does less data exposure matter more?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.
consumer.page: Round 7 personal precedence extended in Round 9 to the shared decision page for every live category.

products.name: Bitwarden
products.description: A leading open-source password manager with public source, recurring third-party audits, a generous free tier, and optional self-hosting.

privacy.note: Bitwarden's security white paper describes end-to-end encryption with vault data encrypted before leaving the device.

transparency.note: Bitwarden publishes recurring third-party audit and certification information, including 2024 and 2025 assessments.

openness.note: Bitwarden publishes its source code and server/client repositories publicly.

security.note: Annual third-party audits cover source code, apps, servers and web properties, with recent 2025 assessments published.

accessibility.note: Bitwarden has a broad free tier plus low-cost paid plans and self-hosting options.

products.name: KeePassXC
products.description: A fully local open-source vault for people comfortable managing sync and backups themselves.

privacy.note: KeePassXC stores an encrypted local database and does not require vendor cloud sync.

transparency.note: KeePassXC lists public security reviews and certifications on its audits page.

openness.note: KeePassXC is GPL-licensed open-source software with public development on GitHub.

security.note: KeePassXC's audits page lists an ANSSI Security Visa dated 2025 and valid until 2028, plus a 2023 independent application security review.

accessibility.note: KeePassXC is free and cross-platform, but manual vault sync and backup make it less effortless than cloud managers.

products.name: KeePass
products.description: The classic local open-source password vault: very private if you can manage files, backups and sync yourself.

privacy.note: KeePass stores passwords in a local encrypted database unlocked by a master key, with no vendor cloud required.

transparency.note: KeePass documents its database security model, encryption algorithms and key-derivation options publicly.

openness.note: KeePass is free and open-source software with source code available from the official project.

security.note: KeePass supports AES, ChaCha20 and Twofish database encryption plus Argon2 key derivation in KeePass 2.x.

accessibility.note: KeePass is free, but mainstream users must handle sync, backups, plugins and cross-device workflows themselves.

products.name: KeePassDX
products.description: A free open-source Android KeePass client for people who want a local vault on mobile without a vendor cloud account.

privacy.note: KeePassDX stores credentials in a local KeePass-format database and does not require a vendor cloud service.

transparency.note: The project documents its local-vault design and public source, though it does not have the independent audit trail of KeePassXC or Bitwarden.

openness.note: KeePassDX is GPLv3 open-source software and says its main safety features remain free for all users.

security.note: KeePassDX supports KeePass KDB/KDBX files with AES, Twofish, ChaCha20 and Argon2, but users still manage file sync and backups themselves.

accessibility.note: It is free, ad-free and Android-native, but local vault sync is less automatic than a mainstream cloud password manager.

products.name: KeePass2Android
products.description: An Android KeePass client with open-source code, local database control, and built-in sync options for people using KeePass across devices.

privacy.note: KeePass2Android stores secrets in a KeePass-compatible database file secured with a strong key, rather than a vendor-hosted vault by default.

transparency.note: The project documents its KeePass-compatible design and sync model publicly on GitHub, though it has less audit depth than leading audited managers.

openness.note: KeePass2Android publishes its app source code publicly and is described as an open-source Android password manager.

security.note: Security inherits KeePass-format encryption strengths, but users remain responsible for sync provider choice, backups and device hygiene.

accessibility.note: KeePass2Android is available through Google Play and supports built-in cloud-storage sync, making KeePass more practical on Android.

products.name: KeePassium
products.description: An audited open-source KeePass-compatible manager for iPhone, iPad and Mac, with user-controlled storage and a usable free tier.

privacy.note: KeePassium is designed to work offline, store data in an encrypted KeePass file and let users choose where that file lives.

transparency.note: KeePassium publishes source code and audit details, including a 2024 Cure53 audit and CASA Tier 2 report.

openness.note: KeePassium is GPLv3 commercial open-source software with buildable source published on GitHub.

security.note: The 2024 Cure53 audit reviewed source code over 10 days and KeePassium says the identified issues were fixed in the next update.

accessibility.note: KeePassium can be used for free, but it is limited to Apple's platforms and keeps some convenience features in paid tiers.

products.name: Strongbox
products.description: A polished KeePass/Password Safe client for iPhone, iPad and Mac with user-controlled storage and strong Apple-platform convenience, but source availability is not OSI-open-source.

privacy.note: Strongbox lets users store KeePass/Password Safe databases anywhere they choose, online or offline, including their own server or cloud provider.

transparency.note: Strongbox publishes functional source for inspection, while its repo clarifies the app is better described as source-available rather than OSI-open-source.

openness.note: The public repo says the release is not OSI-compliant because some non-code/build materials are withheld, so openness is partial.

security.note: Strongbox supports KeePass and Password Safe formats plus hardware-key, biometric, passkey and strong KDF options, but lacks the audit depth of top audited leaders.

accessibility.note: Strongbox has a free version for non-commercial use and paid Pro plans, but it is limited to Apple's platforms.

products.name: Password Safe
products.description: The classic Bruce Schneier-designed local encrypted password safe: simple, open source and private, but less modern than newer cross-device managers.

privacy.note: Password Safe keeps passwords in a local encrypted safe unlocked by a single master password, with no hosted vault requirement.

transparency.note: Password Safe is a public open-source project, but has less modern audit and UX documentation than newer leaders.

openness.note: The official site describes Password Safe as free open-source software, and its source is available on GitHub.

security.note: Schneier's Password Safe page describes the original design and Twofish-based security review, while current security depends on maintained clients and user backup discipline.

accessibility.note: Password Safe is free and available for desktop platforms, but its local-file workflow is less approachable than modern cloud managers.

products.name: pass (password-store)
products.description: A tiny Unix password manager that stores each secret as a GPG-encrypted file and can sync through Git.

privacy.note: pass stores each password in a local GPG-encrypted file, with no vendor cloud by default.

transparency.note: Its design is deliberately small and public: shell scripts, GPG, Git and a simple directory layout.

openness.note: password-store is free software with public source code.

security.note: Security depends heavily on GPG key hygiene, device security and sync choices rather than a managed service.

accessibility.note: The CLI/GPG/Git workflow is powerful but too technical for most mainstream users.

products.name: gopass
products.description: A command-line password and secrets manager for developers and teams, using GPG and Git for local control and collaboration.

privacy.note: gopass stores secrets locally under user control and uses GPG for end-to-end encryption.

transparency.note: The project publicly documents its Git/GPG model, command-line design and source code.

openness.note: gopass describes itself as free, open-source and extensible, with public source on GitHub.

security.note: By default credentials are encrypted with GPG and versioned in Git, but security depends heavily on GPG key hygiene and repository controls.

accessibility.note: gopass supports macOS, Linux, Windows and browser integration, but its CLI-first workflow is for technical users.

products.name: Vaultwarden (self-hosted)
products.description: A community Bitwarden-compatible server for people who want to self-host their password manager backend.

privacy.note: Vaultwarden lets users host their own Bitwarden-compatible server, reducing dependence on a third-party cloud.

transparency.note: The project is public and community-maintained, with issues, code and deployment docs visible.

openness.note: Vaultwarden is open source and Bitwarden API-compatible.

security.note: Security depends on server hardening, patching and admin practice, as reflected in its hardening guide.

accessibility.note: Self-hosting gives control, but requires server administration and maintenance skills.

products.name: Passbolt
products.description: An OpenPGP-based password and credential manager built for teams that want self-hosting and granular sharing.

privacy.note: Passbolt uses end-to-end OpenPGP encryption and offers self-hosted deployment options.

transparency.note: Passbolt publishes security-model documentation and audit information on its security page.

openness.note: Passbolt server code is public on GitHub and the community edition is open source.

security.note: Passbolt reports white-box audits and security testing for its browser extension and API.

accessibility.note: Passbolt is strong for teams, but setup/admin overhead is higher than consumer-first managers.

products.name: Psono
products.description: An open-source, self-hostable password manager for teams that want sharing workflows without a fully proprietary vault.

privacy.note: Psono says vault data is encrypted client-side before storage, including in self-hosted deployments.

transparency.note: Psono publishes security documentation covering encryption layers, rights management, testing and compliance.

openness.note: Psono describes its core as open source and self-hostable, with public server code available.

security.note: Psono supports client-side encryption, MFA options and security reports, but has less public audit depth than top audited leaders.

accessibility.note: Psono can be self-hosted or used as a service, but team administration and server setup are heavier than consumer managers.

products.name: Padloc
products.description: An open-source, end-to-end encrypted password manager for individuals, families and teams, with a clean hosted app model and a slower public release cadence.

privacy.note: Padloc says all sensitive information is end-to-end encrypted, so its servers should not be able to read vault contents.

transparency.note: Padloc publishes a security whitepaper, source code and audit claims, including a recent Radically Open Security audit reference.

openness.note: Padloc's repository describes it as a modern open-source password manager and lists AGPL-3.0 licensing.

security.note: The security model is strong on paper and audited, but the public GitHub release cadence appears slower than the most active leaders.

accessibility.note: Padloc has web, desktop, mobile and browser-extension options plus a free plan with unlimited vault items and devices.

products.name: Zoho Vault
products.description: A business-oriented proprietary password manager with zero-knowledge claims, audit trails and low per-user pricing.

privacy.note: Zoho Vault says it uses zero-knowledge architecture and encrypts confidential data with AES-256.

transparency.note: Zoho Vault publishes security and audit-trail details, including real-time auditing of sensitive changes.

openness.note: Zoho Vault is a proprietary SaaS product, so source-code openness is low.

security.note: Security posture is strong for teams: AES-256, MFA, SSO and audit trails are core product claims.

accessibility.note: Zoho Vault starts at low per-user pricing and fits teams already using Zoho, but is less consumer-simple than Bitwarden or 1Password.

products.name: Proton Pass
products.description: A privacy-company password manager with open-source apps, Cure53 auditing, Proton's 2025 SOC 2 Type II attestation, and a generous free tier.

privacy.note: Proton Pass says it uses end-to-end encryption for passwords, aliases, notes and other vault data.

transparency.note: Proton publishes Pass source links and says Cure53 tested its mobile apps, browser extensions and API.

openness.note: Proton Pass keeps public client repositories and says open source lets users inspect how the apps work.

security.note: Proton completed a SOC 2 Type II audit in 2025, adding operational security validation to Pass's product-level audit record.

accessibility.note: Proton Pass has a free plan and paid options, making it accessible without requiring a paid Proton bundle.

products.name: LessPass
products.description: A stateless password generator that recomputes site passwords from a site, login, and master password instead of syncing a vault.

privacy.note: LessPass does not store a synced vault; passwords are generated from local inputs.

transparency.note: The stateless model is documented publicly, but the approach is less familiar than vault managers.

openness.note: LessPass is GPLv3 open-source software.

security.note: Stateless generation avoids a vault breach target, but password changes and recovery require disciplined parameter tracking.

accessibility.note: LessPass is free and can work offline, but the mental model is less beginner-friendly than a normal vault.

products.name: 1Password
products.description: A polished commercial manager with excellent security architecture, fresh audit materials, and strong usability, but proprietary code and no free tier.

privacy.note: 1Password's Secret Key design means both the account password and device-generated Secret Key protect vault access.

transparency.note: 1Password publishes independent security assessment information and is moving annual penetration-test reports into its Trust Center.

openness.note: 1Password is proprietary, so users rely on audits and documentation rather than public source review.

security.note: Its 2026 security design white paper documents the membership architecture, including Secret Keys, key derivation and sharing design.

accessibility.note: 1Password is highly polished across platforms, but its normal long-term use is paid rather than free-tier based.

products.name: Keeper
products.description: A polished proprietary password manager with a strong compliance posture and zero-knowledge security claims.

privacy.note: Keeper describes a zero-knowledge model in which vault records are encrypted locally before sync.

transparency.note: Keeper publishes security, encryption and compliance information, but the product is proprietary.

openness.note: Keeper is a closed-source commercial product, so audit/compliance evidence substitutes for source inspection.

security.note: Keeper reports strong encryption, compliance certifications and security controls for its commercial platform.

accessibility.note: Keeper is polished and cross-platform, but normal use is paid rather than built around a generous free tier.

products.name: Apple Passwords / iCloud Keychain
products.description: Apple's built-in password manager is convenient and strongly integrated, but best for people staying in Apple's ecosystem.

privacy.note: Apple's iCloud data security overview lists iCloud Keychain as end-to-end encrypted.

transparency.note: Apple publishes security architecture detail, but the password manager itself remains proprietary.

openness.note: Apple Passwords/iCloud Keychain is not open source; trust comes from platform security and documentation.

security.note: Deep OS integration, passkeys and end-to-end encrypted iCloud Keychain support a strong built-in security posture.

accessibility.note: Apple Passwords is free and built in for Apple users, but cross-platform experience is weaker outside Apple's ecosystem.

products.name: Samsung Pass
products.description: Samsung's built-in biometric sign-in and credential manager for Galaxy devices, very convenient inside that ecosystem but not a transparent cross-platform vault.

privacy.note: Samsung says Samsung Pass uses biometric authentication for websites and apps, but the feature is tied to Samsung account and device services.

transparency.note: Samsung explains the biometric login flow and Knox protection, but publishes less vault-specific architecture detail than specialist password managers.

openness.note: Samsung Pass is a proprietary Galaxy platform service rather than an open-source password manager.

security.note: Samsung says data inside Samsung Pass is safeguarded by Samsung Knox and accessed through biometrics.

accessibility.note: Samsung Pass is built into supported Galaxy phones and tablets, but compatible apps, features and regions vary.

products.name: Firefox Passwords
products.description: Mozilla's built-in browser password manager: free and privacy-respecting, but less full-featured than a dedicated vault.

privacy.note: Firefox Sync says synced data, including saved passwords, is encrypted on Mozilla servers so Mozilla cannot read it.

transparency.note: Mozilla documents Firefox's built-in password management and sync behavior publicly.

openness.note: Firefox itself is open source, but the browser password manager is still tied to the Firefox/Mozilla account workflow.

security.note: Firefox password sync is encrypted, but a browser-built-in manager has fewer dedicated vault controls than specialist managers.

accessibility.note: Firefox Passwords is free and built into the browser, making it a low-friction upgrade from password reuse.

products.name: Microsoft Password Manager / Edge
products.description: The built-in Microsoft/Edge option: extremely accessible, but proprietary and tied to the Microsoft account/browser ecosystem.

privacy.note: Microsoft Password Manager stores and syncs credentials through Microsoft account and Edge flows, so privacy depends on that ecosystem.

transparency.note: Microsoft documents Edge password storage and protection, including local disk encryption details.

openness.note: Microsoft Password Manager and Edge account sync are proprietary platform features.

security.note: Edge stores passwords encrypted on disk using AES with OS-protected keys, a solid baseline but not a dedicated open vault model.

accessibility.note: It is free and built into Edge/Windows account flows, so it is one of the easiest ways for Microsoft users to stop reusing passwords.

products.name: Enpass
products.description: A local-vault password manager that lets users choose their own cloud sync, but remains proprietary.

privacy.note: Enpass says vault data is stored locally or in the user's chosen cloud, not on Enpass servers.

transparency.note: Enpass publishes security and privacy details, but less audit/compliance depth than top commercial peers.

openness.note: Enpass is proprietary despite its local-vault approach.

security.note: The local-vault model and documented encryption are solid, but public audit depth is thinner than leaders.

accessibility.note: Enpass offers free and paid personal options, including lifetime-style paid positioning in some markets.

products.name: Sticky Password
products.description: A long-running proprietary manager whose distinctive value is letting users sync locally over Wi-Fi instead of the vendor cloud.

privacy.note: Sticky Password lets users choose cloud sync, local Wi-Fi sync or manual offline sync, keeping more control over where vault data travels.

transparency.note: Sticky Password publishes feature/security materials, but public independent audit depth is limited.

openness.note: Sticky Password is proprietary, so source-code openness is low despite the local-sync option.

security.note: Sticky Password says encrypted data can sync by cloud, local Wi-Fi or manual offline methods using AES-256.

accessibility.note: Sticky Password offers trials and paid annual/lifetime-style plans, but has less ecosystem polish than the largest managers.

products.name: NordPass
products.description: A mainstream proprietary password manager with zero-knowledge claims, a free plan and business audit evidence.

privacy.note: NordPass describes a zero-knowledge architecture using client-side encryption before data reaches servers.

transparency.note: NordPass currently cites a Cure53 audit, but users still rely on vendor-published assurance rather than open source.

openness.note: NordPass is closed source, so users rely on vendor documentation and audits rather than source review.

security.note: NordPass says its Cure53 audit covered cryptographic premise, source code, background app and codebase.

accessibility.note: NordPass offers free and paid personal plans and simple apps.

products.name: Dashlane
products.description: A polished proprietary password manager with a clear security white paper and paid-product focus.

privacy.note: Dashlane describes a zero-knowledge architecture where only users can decrypt vault contents.

transparency.note: Dashlane publishes security white paper and security-program information, but the product remains proprietary.

openness.note: Dashlane is closed source, limiting independent community review compared with open managers.

security.note: The zero-knowledge white paper and security program support a good commercial security score.

accessibility.note: Dashlane is polished and cross-platform, but the strongest feature set is paid.

products.name: RoboForm
products.description: A long-running proprietary password manager with affordable plans and less public audit depth than leaders.

privacy.note: RoboForm states data is encrypted locally, while its privacy policy still covers account and service data processing.

transparency.note: RoboForm publishes security and privacy pages, but public independent audit depth is limited.

openness.note: RoboForm is proprietary, so users cannot inspect source code like Bitwarden or KeePassXC.

security.note: RoboForm is long-running and documents local encryption, but lacks the public audit story of the strongest peers.

accessibility.note: RoboForm has a free plan and inexpensive personal plans, though free use has device limitations.

products.name: Google Password Manager
products.description: The default Chrome/Android option: very accessible, but tied to Google's account and platform ecosystem.

privacy.note: Google Password Manager stores passwords in a Google Account, making privacy depend on Google's account ecosystem.

transparency.note: Google documents password management and checkup features, but the manager is proprietary.

openness.note: Google Password Manager is built into proprietary Google account/Chrome/Android services.

security.note: Google Password Checkup warns users about compromised passwords and risky credentials.

accessibility.note: It is free and built into Chrome and Android, making it one of the easiest options to start using.

products.name: Norton Password Manager
products.description: A free proprietary password manager tied to Norton's security ecosystem, with strong zero-knowledge claims but little source transparency.

privacy.note: Norton says vault data is encrypted locally before cloud storage and that the vault password is never stored or sent to its server.

transparency.note: Norton documents its zero-knowledge architecture and AES-256 vault design, but does not provide open-source client review.

openness.note: Norton Password Manager is proprietary and presented through Norton apps/extensions rather than public source code.

security.note: The support article cites AES-256 encryption, local decryption, 2FA support and brute-force protections for the vault.

accessibility.note: Norton offers the password manager as a free standalone extension and includes it in Norton 360 plans.

products.name: Avira Password Manager
products.description: A simple Gen Digital/Avira password manager with cloud sync and AES-256 claims, best read as convenience security rather than audit-led trust.

privacy.note: Avira's app listing says passwords, cards and notes are protected with 256-bit AES and that not even Avira can access the data.

transparency.note: Avira documents the free and registered versions, including cloud backup/sync, but has a thinner password-manager audit trail than leaders.

openness.note: Avira Password Manager is proprietary and distributed as Avira web, browser-extension and mobile apps.

security.note: The app listing cites AES-256 vault protection, biometric unlock on Apple devices and a security-status feature.

accessibility.note: Avira offers web, extension and mobile access with free registration and paid Pro features.

products.name: Bitdefender SecurePass
products.description: Bitdefender's replacement for its discontinued Password Manager, with end-to-end encryption claims and broad platform support.

privacy.note: Bitdefender says SecurePass provides end-to-end data encryption for credentials and sensitive information.

transparency.note: Bitdefender publicly documents the migration from the discontinued Password Manager to SecurePass, including lifecycle dates.

openness.note: Bitdefender says SecurePass is built on open-source technology, but it is presented as a proprietary Bitdefender service.

security.note: SecurePass adds passkey-era features, password generation and strength advice, but it is newer than the most established audited managers.

accessibility.note: SecurePass supports Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and major browsers, with upgrade paths for existing Bitdefender Password Manager users.

products.name: Kaspersky Password Manager
products.description: A mainstream security-suite password manager with encrypted-vault claims, but serious trust and availability penalties from past generator flaws and US restrictions.

privacy.note: Kaspersky says the main password encrypts the data vault and the vault syncs through a My Kaspersky account.

transparency.note: Kaspersky documents AES/PBKDF2 vault protection, but external reporting and US restrictions complicate trust for many users.

openness.note: Kaspersky Password Manager is proprietary and relies on vendor documentation rather than public client source review.

security.note: Kaspersky's advisory list documents CVE-2020-27020 as a fixed Password Manager generator weakness, so the old flaw remains a track-record penalty even if patched.

accessibility.note: The US Commerce Department's Kaspersky prohibition took effect in 2024 and continues to make Kaspersky software unsuitable for US users because sales and updates are barred for U.S. persons.

products.name: mSecure
products.description: A long-running password manager with AES-256, zero-knowledge claims and flexible sync, but less public audit depth than leading options.

privacy.note: mSecure says data is encrypted before leaving the device and that only the user can unlock it.

transparency.note: mSecure publishes a security-model support article and feature pages, but no current public third-party audit page was found.

openness.note: mSecure is proprietary software rather than a source-reviewable open-source manager.

security.note: mSecure cites AES-256 encryption, an account key and zero-knowledge architecture across devices.

accessibility.note: mSecure has mobile and desktop apps with modest paid tiers and a trial/free path, but fewer ecosystem advantages than built-ins.

products.name: Password Boss
products.description: A proprietary manager now aimed heavily at business and MSP use, with client-side encryption claims but limited public audit depth.

privacy.note: Password Boss says all user data is encrypted and decrypted locally using AES-256.

transparency.note: Password Boss publishes security claims, but its pricing and assurance material are less transparent than consumer leaders.

openness.note: Password Boss is proprietary and does not offer public source review.

security.note: Password Boss cites AES-256, PBKDF2-derived keys, zero-knowledge architecture and 2FA, but not a current public independent audit.

accessibility.note: Password Boss offers trials and business/MSP flows, but the legacy desktop download page now points new users to the WebApp path.

products.name: SafeInCloud / Safe
products.description: A proprietary local-vault password manager that syncs through user-chosen clouds and leans on AES-256/zero-knowledge claims.

privacy.note: SafeInCloud says it does not store or know passwords and that vault contents are encrypted on-device under a zero-knowledge policy.

transparency.note: SafeInCloud publishes privacy, terms and feature pages, but no current public third-party audit page was found.

openness.note: SafeInCloud is proprietary; its terms reserve rights to the app code and brand to SafeInCloud SAS.

security.note: SafeInCloud documents AES-256 protection and PBKDF2 key derivation for brute-force resistance.

accessibility.note: SafeInCloud offers desktop/mobile apps, autofill, breach checks and user-controlled cloud sync.

products.name: Secrets
products.description: An Apple-ecosystem password manager that stores locally or via iCloud rather than vendor servers, but remains proprietary and platform-limited.

privacy.note: Secrets says passwords and information are never synced with its servers; optional sync uses encrypted iCloud storage.

transparency.note: Secrets documents iCloud-only sync support, but does not provide the audit depth or public source of top-tier managers.

openness.note: Secrets is proprietary Apple-platform software rather than an open-source password manager.

security.note: The App Store listing cites 256-bit encryption, biometrics, passphrase protection and automatic locking.

accessibility.note: Secrets is polished for iPhone, iPad and Mac users, but the iCloud-centered model limits appeal outside Apple ecosystems.

products.name: Buttercup
products.description: A once-promising open-source password manager whose maintainer announced the project was ending, so it now belongs in the migration-caution bucket.

privacy.note: Buttercup stores encrypted vault files that can live locally or in user-chosen storage rather than a required vendor cloud.

transparency.note: Buttercup's GitHub organization now flags project closure and says the repositories are transitioning into public archives.

openness.note: Buttercup is a GPL-licensed open-source password manager with public repositories.

security.note: The open encrypted-vault design is useful, but public-archive status creates a serious maintenance risk for security software.

accessibility.note: Existing public repositories remain available, but the archived status means users should treat Buttercup as a migration-caution option.

products.name: AuthPass
products.description: A free open-source KeePass-compatible app for people who want local KDBX control with mobile and desktop clients.

privacy.note: AuthPass stores passwords in the open KeePass format where the user chooses, and says it does not send passwords to its servers.

transparency.note: AuthPass publishes docs, source code and issue tracking, but has less audit evidence than KeePassXC or Bitwarden.

openness.note: AuthPass is GPL-3.0 open-source software with public GitHub development.

security.note: AuthPass relies on the KeePass KDBX format and supports local/user-controlled storage, but lacks a prominent independent audit trail.

accessibility.note: AuthPass is free across Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and Windows, with no ads or subscriptions in its Play listing.

products.name: KeeWeb
products.description: A web/desktop KeePass-compatible manager that can be self-hosted, useful for technical users who understand its maintenance and deployment tradeoffs.

privacy.note: KeeWeb opens or creates KeePass KDBX databases and lets users store vault files locally or in chosen cloud storage.

transparency.note: KeeWeb is public on GitHub with visible repository history, issues and self-hosting documentation.

openness.note: KeeWeb is open source and publishes its web, desktop and self-hosting materials in public repositories.

security.note: The KDBX-compatible model is strong when maintained and deployed carefully, but a browser/web vault adds more operational surface than KeePassXC.

accessibility.note: KeeWeb can run as a desktop app or browser app and can be self-hosted, but setup is more technical than mainstream cloud managers.

products.name: TeamPass
products.description: A free self-hosted team password manager with GPL licensing and role controls, but a heavier operational and patching burden.

privacy.note: TeamPass is installed on-premise, but its own docs note that passwords/custom fields are encrypted while other database fields are clear text.

transparency.note: TeamPass publishes a website, documentation, public repository and security contact, but users must track patches closely.

openness.note: TeamPass is distributed as open-source GPL-3.0 software.

security.note: Recent vulnerability records such as CVE-2023-1545 show why self-hosted TeamPass requires active patch management.

accessibility.note: TeamPass is powerful for teams but requires server operation, database setup and admin discipline.

products.name: OneKeePass
products.description: A newer cross-platform KeePass-compatible manager for people who want local vault control with modern desktop and mobile clients.

privacy.note: OneKeePass stores secrets in a KeePass-compatible KDBX file that can live locally or in user-chosen storage.

transparency.note: OneKeePass publishes public desktop and mobile repositories, but does not appear to publish the same formal audit trail as larger managers.

openness.note: The OneKeePass desktop repository describes it as a cross-platform open-source password manager supporting KDBX 4.x.

security.note: KDBX local-vault design is strong, but the project is newer and less independently audited than KeePassXC or Bitwarden.

accessibility.note: OneKeePass is available across desktop and mobile, but users still need to manage vault storage and sync choices.

products.name: QtPass
products.description: A graphical interface for the standard Unix pass password store, best for technical users already comfortable with GPG and Git.

privacy.note: QtPass uses pass, where passwords are stored as GPG-encrypted files under user control.

transparency.note: QtPass publishes a public GitHub repository and project documentation, but not a large formal audit program.

openness.note: QtPass describes itself as open source and free.

security.note: The pass/GPG model is mature, but safe operation depends on GPG key hygiene, sync choices and user discipline.

accessibility.note: QtPass adds a GUI and multi-platform support, but the underlying pass/GPG workflow is still more technical than mainstream managers.

products.name: Clipperz
products.description: A long-running zero-knowledge web password manager that can also be inspected and self-hosted, though it feels more niche than modern consumer tools.

privacy.note: Clipperz describes itself as a zero-knowledge web application that cannot inspect user data.

transparency.note: Clipperz publishes open-source project information and code links for inspecting or running the password manager.

openness.note: Clipperz says its password manager is AGPLv3 open source and hosted on GitHub.

security.note: The zero-knowledge model is privacy-friendly, but the web-vault design and age of the project make current security review less clear.

accessibility.note: Clipperz can be used from a browser without installation and has an offline version, but it is more niche than mainstream autofill managers.

products.name: Spectre
products.description: A privacy-first deterministic password app that stores no vault, useful for a narrow threat model but less forgiving than a normal manager.

privacy.note: Spectre calculates passwords when needed instead of storing or sending a password vault.

transparency.note: Spectre documents its algorithm and publishes source-code information for the website and implementations.

openness.note: Spectre says it is open-source Free Software with fully open and auditable code.

security.note: A deterministic-password-manager review remains the clearest caution for Spectre's model: derivation-parameter exposure, breach-notification gaps, rotation friction and protocol-upgrade tradeoffs versus vault managers.

accessibility.note: Spectre is free and cross-platform in principle, but its stateless model is less familiar and harder to recover from mistakes than a vault.

products.name: Passwarden
products.description: A commercial password manager built around client-side encryption, often bundled with a broader privacy/security suite.

privacy.note: Passwarden says vault data is encrypted client-side and can be decrypted only with the user's Master Password.

transparency.note: Passwarden publishes consumer security explanations, but source code and independent audit detail are limited compared with open managers.

openness.note: Passwarden is a proprietary commercial password manager rather than an open-source vault.

security.note: Client-side encryption is a strong baseline, but public security-audit evidence is less visible than for Bitwarden, 1Password or KeePassXC.

accessibility.note: Passwarden offers consumer apps and is bundled with MonoDefense, but it is less ubiquitous than the major free-tier managers.

products.name: LogMeOnce
products.description: A feature-heavy password manager with many passwordless and MFA options, but a less transparent security posture than leading audited tools.

privacy.note: LogMeOnce says it uses zero-knowledge technology and does not know a user's encryption key or actual passwords.

transparency.note: LogMeOnce publishes support articles and feature documentation, but source code and independent audit detail are not prominent.

openness.note: LogMeOnce is a proprietary password manager, not an open-source vault.

security.note: The product emphasizes passwordless login and many MFA methods, but public third-party audit evidence is less visible than for top-tier managers.

accessibility.note: LogMeOnce offers mobile and desktop access and a free route, making it easier to adopt than enterprise-only vaults.

products.name: SAASPASS
products.description: A password manager wrapped around dynamic passwords and MFA, more identity-security oriented than a simple personal vault.

privacy.note: SAASPASS provides a password manager and dynamic-password model, but privacy architecture details are less explicit than leading zero-knowledge vaults.

transparency.note: SAASPASS publishes product pages for password management and MFA but limited public source or audit detail.

openness.note: SAASPASS is a proprietary security service rather than an open-source password manager.

security.note: SAASPASS emphasizes dynamic passwords and MFA as added protection against static-password attacks.

accessibility.note: SAASPASS supports common websites and services, but its model is more complex than a mainstream autofill manager.

products.name: Password Depot
products.description: A German commercial password and secrets manager for teams, with strong enterprise controls but limited open-source transparency.

privacy.note: Password Depot positions passwords and confidential files as centrally stored, encrypted, access-controlled and traceable.

transparency.note: AceBIT publishes a Trust Center and ISO 27001-related materials, but the product is not open-source.

openness.note: Password Depot is proprietary commercial software rather than an open-source password manager.

security.note: Enterprise Server materials emphasize access control, strong authentication, encryption and audit logging.

accessibility.note: Password Depot is more accessible to managed teams than individuals because its strongest features are enterprise/server oriented.

products.name: Pleasant Password Server
products.description: A self-hosted multi-user password server compatible with KeePass and Password Safe clients, aimed at organizations rather than casual users.

privacy.note: Pleasant Password Server is locally hosted and gives administrators control over access to individual passwords and folders.

transparency.note: Pleasant publishes product features and compatibility details, but not open-source code or a prominent independent audit trail.

openness.note: The server is proprietary, though it is compatible with KeePass Password Safe and Bruce Schneier's Password Safe clients.

security.note: Role and folder access controls plus self-hosting are useful, but organizations carry server-hardening and patch-management responsibility.

accessibility.note: Pleasant supports web, browser extension, mobile and desktop access, but setup is an organizational server project.

products.name: ManageEngine Password Manager Pro
products.description: A Zoho/ManageEngine privileged-account vault for IT teams, strong on governance but complex and enterprise-centered.

privacy.note: ManageEngine describes Password Manager Pro as a centralized vault with granular access controls for privileged accounts.

transparency.note: ManageEngine publishes security specifications and product documentation, but the product is not open-source.

openness.note: Password Manager Pro is proprietary enterprise software rather than an open-source password vault.

security.note: Security specifications cite AES-256 encryption, installation-specific master keys, auditing and enterprise controls.

accessibility.note: Password Manager Pro is built for IT and privileged-access management, so ordinary consumer accessibility is low.

products.name: Securden Password Vault
products.description: A self-hosted enterprise password vault with auditing, access workflows and privileged-account controls for IT teams.

privacy.note: Securden describes Password Vault for Enterprises as a web-based, on-premise self-hosted software solution.

transparency.note: Securden publishes architecture, feature and audit-trail documentation, but the vault itself is proprietary.

openness.note: Securden Password Vault is proprietary enterprise software rather than open-source code users can inspect.

security.note: Securden emphasizes granular access workflows, audit trails, reporting and privileged-account controls.

accessibility.note: Securden is useful for IT teams, but deployment and administration are enterprise tasks rather than consumer setup.

products.name: Delinea Secret Server
products.description: A mature privileged-access and secrets vault for organizations managing admin, service, machine and application credentials.

privacy.note: Delinea positions Secret Server as an enterprise vault for privileged accounts, machine identities, DevOps and AI-agent credentials.

transparency.note: Delinea publishes product and documentation pages for vaulting, discovery, rotation and session monitoring.

openness.note: Secret Server is proprietary enterprise PAM software, not an open-source password manager.

security.note: Secret Server includes discovery, password rotation, session monitoring and enterprise vault controls for privileged credentials.

accessibility.note: Secret Server is powerful for managed organizations but expensive and complex for ordinary individuals or small households.

products.name: 2FAS Auth
products.description: A polished local-first authenticator app with public source, no required account, cloud/manual backups and a strong privacy posture.

privacy.note: 2FAS says Auth can be used without an account, stores tokens locally, and does not collect or see user data unless users choose otherwise.

transparency.note: 2FAS publishes public source repositories and describes its local-first, zero-knowledge design on its product site.

openness.note: 2FAS publishes its Auth iOS app, browser extension and related repositories publicly.

security.note: 2FAS emphasizes local on-device encryption, optional backups, browser-extension pairing and offline token storage.

accessibility.note: 2FAS Auth is free, available on iOS and Android, and designed as a mainstream authenticator rather than an admin tool.

products.name: Aegis Authenticator
products.description: A strong Android-only authenticator with encrypted local vaults, imports/exports and open-source code.

privacy.note: Aegis stores tokens in a secure local vault and supports user-controlled import/export rather than mandatory cloud sync.

transparency.note: Aegis documents AES-256-GCM vault encryption, unlock options and supported HOTP/TOTP standards in its public repository.

openness.note: Aegis is GPL-licensed open-source Android software with public code and issue tracking.

security.note: Aegis supports encrypted vaults, password or biometric unlock, screen-capture prevention and standard HOTP/TOTP algorithms.

accessibility.note: Aegis is free and polished for Android, but it is not a cross-platform iOS/Desktop option.

products.name: Ente Auth
products.description: A free, open-source authenticator with end-to-end encrypted backups and sync across mobile, desktop and web.

privacy.note: Ente Auth provides end-to-end encrypted backups and sync so tokens do not need to be visible to the service provider.

transparency.note: Ente says its source code and cryptography have been externally audited by Cure53, Symbolic Software and Fallible.

openness.note: Ente publishes its monorepo under AGPL-3.0 and describes Auth as fully open source.

security.note: Ente Auth combines standard authenticator codes with end-to-end encrypted cloud backups and cross-platform sync.

accessibility.note: Ente Auth is free and works across mobile, desktop and web, with import/export to reduce lock-in.

products.name: Proton Authenticator
products.description: A newer cross-platform 2FA app from Proton with offline access, end-to-end encrypted sync and no required Proton account.

privacy.note: Proton says Authenticator can sync 2FA codes across devices with end-to-end encryption or stay local, with no account required.

transparency.note: Proton describes Authenticator as open source and says users can import from other apps or export from Proton Authenticator.

openness.note: Proton says Authenticator is open source, continuing the transparency model used across Proton services.

security.note: Proton Authenticator supports offline codes, end-to-end encrypted sync, automatic backups and biometric or PIN protection.

accessibility.note: Proton Authenticator is free on desktop and mobile apps and works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

products.name: YubiKey 5 Series
products.description: A mature multi-protocol hardware security key for FIDO2/WebAuthn, passkeys, smart card, OTP and OpenPGP workflows, strongest for people willing to buy and manage backup keys.

privacy.note: YubiKey 5 stores authentication material on a separate hardware key rather than in a cloud password account or browser profile.

transparency.note: Yubico publishes detailed product and protocol documentation for YubiKey 5, including supported interfaces and authentication standards.

openness.note: YubiKey 5 is well documented around standards support, but the commercial product pages do not present it as open-source hardware or firmware.

security.note: YubiKey 5 supports FIDO2/WebAuthn, FIDO U2F, smart card, OTP and OpenPGP, enabling phishing-resistant and hardware-backed login.

accessibility.note: The line offers USB-A, USB-C, NFC and Lightning form factors, but users should buy and manage at least one backup key.

products.name: Nitrokey 3
products.description: An open-source and open-hardware security key family with FIDO2/passkey, OpenPGP and password-entry features, strongest for users who value auditability and can handle rougher setup edges.

privacy.note: Nitrokey 3 is a separate hardware authenticator and can be paired with a backup key rather than relying on a single synced account.

transparency.note: Nitrokey publishes user documentation plus firmware repositories for its FIDO2 security-key work.

openness.note: Nitrokey describes Nitrokey 3 as fully open source and open hardware, with no NDA needed for documentation.

security.note: Nitrokey's FIDO2 firmware documentation describes support for FIDO2/U2F, phishing-resistant login and hardware security features.

accessibility.note: Nitrokey 3 supports Windows, Linux, macOS and some Android/iOS use, but passkey/password-entry capacity and setup vary by model.

products.name: Google Titan Security Key
products.description: Google's FIDO security key for phishing-resistant 2FA/passkeys, easy for Google-account protection but proprietary and Google-ecosystem centered.

privacy.note: Titan Security Key uses public-key cryptography so the private key stays on the hardware key during supported sign-in flows.

transparency.note: Google documents Titan's FIDO compatibility, sign-in model, purchase channels and use cases for account-takeover protection.

openness.note: Google describes a hardware chip with Google-engineered firmware rather than an open-hardware or open-firmware device.

security.note: Google positions Titan as phishing-resistant 2FA for services that support FIDO standards, with tamper-resistant hardware.

accessibility.note: Titan is broadly usable with devices, browsers and apps that support FIDO, and Google offers retail and bulk purchasing paths.

products.name: Solo 2
products.description: An open-source FIDO2/WebAuthn security key with public hardware schematics and firmware, appealing to people who want auditability and lower cost over enterprise polish.

privacy.note: Solo 2 is a dedicated hardware key used for FIDO2/WebAuthn login rather than a synced software password vault.

transparency.note: SoloKeys says Solo 2 publishes every circuit, component and design decision, including hardware schematics on GitHub.

openness.note: SoloKeys describes Solo 2 as fully open-source hardware and firmware, with hardware licensed under CERN-OHL-S.

security.note: Solo 2 is a FIDO2/WebAuthn key designed to protect against phishing, account takeover and unauthorized access.

accessibility.note: SoloKeys positions Solo 2 as plug-in, touch-to-authenticate hardware with USB-A and USB-C models and no basic-use software install.

products.name: OnlyKey
products.description: A hybrid hardware password manager, 2FA key and encryption token that can type stored credentials and support FIDO2/U2F/TOTP, but is more niche and setup-heavy than ordinary vaults.

privacy.note: OnlyKey stores passwords and 2FA material on a physical device that can type credentials without a cloud vault.

transparency.note: OnlyKey publishes product explanations for its hardware password-manager, 2FA and encryption-token roles.

openness.note: OnlyKey describes the product as open source and verifiable, while also selling it as a finished hardware device.

security.note: OnlyKey supports FIDO2/U2F, Yubikey OTP, TOTP and challenge-response, and uses PIN protection with erase behavior after repeated failures.

accessibility.note: OnlyKey can enter usernames/passwords and act as a 2FA token, but users must learn a more specialized hardware workflow.

products.name: Token2 FIDO2 Security Keys
products.description: A broad FIDO2 security-key line, including PIN+ and biometric models, useful as a lower-cost or enterprise-compatible alternative to the best-known keys.

privacy.note: Token2 FIDO2 keys provide hardware-backed passwordless or second-factor authentication rather than account-synced secrets.

transparency.note: Token2 publishes compatibility and certification claims, including FIDO Alliance membership and Microsoft-compatible FIDO2 listings.

openness.note: Token2 emphasizes certified, standards-compatible hardware keys, but does not present the line as open-source hardware or firmware.

security.note: Token2 describes its FIDO2 keys as standards-based, phishing-resistant passwordless authentication devices, with PIN+ and biometric models available.

accessibility.note: Token2 sells a broad line of FIDO2 keys and highlights Microsoft Entra/Azure AD compatibility for organizational deployment.

products.name: Yubico Authenticator
products.description: An authenticator app that stores TOTP secrets on a YubiKey, trading setup cost for much stronger portability and hardware-backed protection.

privacy.note: Yubico Authenticator stores credentials on a user's YubiKey rather than primarily in a phone or cloud account.

transparency.note: Yubico publishes detailed product documentation and a public Authenticator app source repository.

openness.note: Yubico publishes the Yubico Authenticator desktop/Android code in a public repository.

security.note: Yubico says credentials stay in the YubiKey secure element and cannot be extracted, giving hardware-backed protection.

accessibility.note: Yubico Authenticator works across major desktop and mobile platforms, but it requires buying and managing compatible YubiKeys.

products.name: Bitwarden Authenticator
products.description: A simple standalone TOTP app from Bitwarden, useful for people who want a familiar authenticator separate from their main vault.

privacy.note: Bitwarden says standalone Authenticator local codes are stored on the device and not synced to Bitwarden servers unless copied/synced into a vault.

transparency.note: Bitwarden documents local storage, backup behavior, code transfer and differences from the integrated vault authenticator.

openness.note: Bitwarden publishes its security products as open-source repositories, though Authenticator inherits the broader Bitwarden codebase context.

security.note: Bitwarden notes Authenticator stores keys in a local unencrypted database protected by device security and optional biometrics, so it is convenient but not the strongest standalone vault design.

accessibility.note: Bitwarden Authenticator is available for iOS and Android and can be used without a Bitwarden Password Manager account.

products.name: FreeOTP
products.description: A simple open-source HOTP/TOTP authenticator from Red Hat, strong on standards but more basic than newer polished 2FA apps.

privacy.note: FreeOTP is a local one-time-password app using HOTP/TOTP standards, with no proprietary server component required for normal use.

transparency.note: FreeOTP publishes Android source code, permissions and standards notes in its public repository.

openness.note: FreeOTP is open source under Apache-2.0, with pull requests welcome on GitHub.

security.note: FreeOTP implements HOTP and TOTP open standards, but it is more basic than encrypted-vault authenticators like Aegis or Ente Auth.

accessibility.note: FreeOTP is free and available on Android and iOS, but its interface and backup story are less friendly than newer mainstream apps.

products.name: Google Authenticator
products.description: The default mainstream authenticator app: easy, free and familiar, but tied to Google sync choices and less transparent than open-source rivals.

privacy.note: Google Authenticator can run without a Google Account, but synced codes are stored in a Google Account and encrypted in Google's systems.

transparency.note: Google documents code sync, accountless use, transfer, privacy screen and recovery behaviors in its help center.

openness.note: The current Google Authenticator app is distributed as a Google product rather than a fully public open-source app stack.

security.note: Google Authenticator generates offline verification codes, supports privacy screen and sync encryption, but it is not phishing-resistant like passkeys or hardware keys.

accessibility.note: Google Authenticator is free, widely recognized and easy to use on Android and iOS.

products.name: Microsoft Authenticator
products.description: A mainstream authenticator and passwordless sign-in app, strongest for Microsoft accounts and workplaces already using Microsoft identity.

privacy.note: Microsoft Authenticator is tightly tied to Microsoft account, work and school sign-in flows rather than a local-only authenticator model.

transparency.note: Microsoft documents Authenticator as a two-factor and passwordless sign-in app, but detailed app internals are not public-source transparent.

openness.note: Microsoft Authenticator is proprietary software distributed by Microsoft.

security.note: Microsoft positions Authenticator for highly secure two-factor authentication and passwordless sign-in across personal, work and school accounts.

accessibility.note: Microsoft Authenticator is free and especially easy for users already in Microsoft 365, Windows or Azure AD ecosystems.

products.name: Authy
products.description: A once-default authenticator with convenient cloud backups, but phone-number dependence, closed source and a 2024 Authy data-exposure alert make it a weaker pick now.

privacy.note: Twilio's 2024 Authy security alert remains the main privacy track-record penalty: attackers identified Authy account data, including phone numbers, through an unauthenticated endpoint.

transparency.note: Twilio disclosed the Authy endpoint incident and asked users to update, but Authy's implementation remains proprietary rather than public-source transparent.

openness.note: Authy is a proprietary Twilio app rather than an open-source authenticator.

security.note: Authy offers secure cloud backup and multi-device support, but the 2024 phone-number exposure and phone-number account model keep its track record below leaders.

accessibility.note: Authy remains free and easy to set up for common 2FA flows.

products.name: Duo Mobile
products.description: A workplace MFA app attached to Cisco Duo identity security, useful and mature but designed around administrator-controlled enterprise access.

privacy.note: Cisco Duo is an identity and access management platform that gives organizations visibility into who accesses what, when and where.

transparency.note: Cisco publishes Duo product pages and identity-security materials, but Duo Mobile is not an open-source authenticator.

openness.note: Duo Mobile is proprietary Cisco software rather than an open-source app.

security.note: Cisco positions Duo around phishing-resistant authentication, identity security and unauthorized-access protection.

accessibility.note: Duo Mobile is easy for enrolled users, but ordinary people usually use it because an employer or school requires Cisco Duo.

products.name: Okta Verify
products.description: A common workplace and campus MFA app with push, codes and biometrics, but tightly bound to organization-managed Okta identity systems.

privacy.note: Okta Verify is used to access organization-managed apps through Okta identity flows rather than a user-controlled local-only model.

transparency.note: Okta documents Verify and passwordless MFA options, including push, codes, biometrics and passkeys/FIDO2 WebAuthn.

openness.note: Okta Verify is proprietary Okta software, not an open-source authenticator app.

security.note: Okta Verify supports push notifications, temporary six-digit codes and biometrics when enabled by an organization.

accessibility.note: Okta Verify is easy for enrolled users, but setup and availability are normally controlled by an employer, school or app administrator.

products.name: LastPass
products.description: A mainstream password manager whose 2022 breach and long-tail vault risk make it the honest floor for security track record.

privacy.note: TechCrunch reported a 2026 Klue supply-chain breach exposed LastPass customer support and sales data, adding phishing risk on top of the 2022 vault-breach history.

transparency.note: LastPass now links incident details and remedial work, but the staged 2022 disclosure and later vault-risk reports keep transparency trust limited.

openness.note: LastPass presents assurance through compliance, audits and architecture docs rather than public source review.

security.note: TechCrunch's 2026 coverage notes the 2022 breach exposed encrypted vaults to offline cracking risk and says later crypto thefts were linked to that breach.

accessibility.note: LastPass remains easy to use and has consumer plans, but free-tier device limits reduce its accessibility edge.

products.name: Infisical
products.description: An open-source developer secrets platform for teams managing API keys, certificates, machine identities and privileged access across infrastructure.

privacy.note: Infisical's secrets-management docs describe centralized management of API keys, database credentials and application configuration across environments.

transparency.note: Infisical publishes a public trust center with security and compliance information.

openness.note: Infisical's GitHub repository describes it as an open-source security infrastructure platform for secrets, certificates and privileged access management.

security.note: Infisical supports machine identities, OIDC workflows and fine-grained access patterns for CI/CD secrets delivery.

accessibility.note: Infisical offers a cloud product and self-hostable open-source path, but it is still aimed at developers and teams rather than ordinary password-vault users.

products.name: OpenBao
products.description: A community-governed open-source fork of Vault for organizations that want strong secrets management without HashiCorp's newer source-available licensing tradeoff.

privacy.note: OpenBao describes itself as an identity-based secrets and encryption management system for tightly controlling access to passwords, certificates and keys.

transparency.note: OpenBao is managed as a community-driven OpenSSF project under the Linux Foundation.

openness.note: OpenBao's GitHub repository is licensed under MPL-2.0 and describes open governance under an OSI-approved open-source license.

security.note: OpenBao docs describe authentication, authorization, auditability and encryption services for controlling sensitive data access.

accessibility.note: OpenBao provides docs and downloads, but operating a Vault-style secrets manager remains a technical infrastructure task.

products.name: HashiCorp Vault
products.description: A mature identity-based secrets manager for infrastructure teams, strong on capability and track record but no longer straightforwardly open source after HashiCorp's BSL shift.

privacy.note: HashiCorp says Vault centrally stores, accesses and distributes secrets to humans, machines, services and AI agents.

transparency.note: HashiCorp publishes Vault product docs and tutorials, but governance and licensing are now controlled by HashiCorp/IBM.

openness.note: HashiCorp announced its move from MPL-2.0 to the Business Source License for future releases of core products including Vault.

security.note: Vault provides access control, detailed audit logs and a unified interface for tightly controlling secrets such as API keys, passwords and certificates.

accessibility.note: Vault has extensive tutorials and managed options, but deploying and operating it well is an advanced infrastructure responsibility.

products.name: SOPS
products.description: A simple open-source encrypted-file workflow for developers who want secrets in Git or config files without storing them in plaintext.

privacy.note: SOPS encrypts YAML, JSON, ENV, INI and binary files using cloud KMS providers, age or PGP.

transparency.note: SOPS publishes documentation and its source repository publicly.

openness.note: The SOPS repository is publicly available under the MPL-2.0 license.

security.note: SOPS supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, HuaweiCloud KMS, age and PGP, making key custody explicit rather than hidden in the tool.

accessibility.note: SOPS is flexible and free, but it is a command-line developer tool rather than a consumer-friendly vault.

products.name: Bitwarden Secrets Manager
products.description: Bitwarden's developer-focused secrets manager for teams that already trust Bitwarden and want infrastructure secrets without switching to a separate enterprise vault.

privacy.note: Bitwarden says Secrets Manager lets developers, DevOps and cybersecurity teams centrally store, manage and deploy secrets at scale.

transparency.note: Bitwarden publishes Secrets Manager docs, SDK docs and recurring audit information for its broader platform.

openness.note: Bitwarden publishes public repositories and documentation for Secrets Manager-related tooling.

security.note: Bitwarden Secrets Manager supports permissions, access tokens and CLI/SDK workflows for deploying secrets.

accessibility.note: Bitwarden notes Secrets Manager is tailored for infrastructure secrets and uses the web app and CLI, not ordinary employee credential autofill.

products.name: 1Password Secrets Automation
products.description: A developer/DevOps extension of 1Password for teams that want application and infrastructure secrets to live in the same commercial trust model as employee vaults.

privacy.note: 1Password says its secrets-management tools store, manage, automate and share application and infrastructure secrets across the development lifecycle.

transparency.note: 1Password publishes developer documentation for Secrets Automation workflows using service accounts or Connect servers.

openness.note: 1Password Secrets Automation is a proprietary commercial add-on rather than an open-source secrets manager.

security.note: 1Password says Secrets Automation can securely access vault items from company apps and cloud infrastructure using a private REST API through Connect.

accessibility.note: The workflow is easier for teams already using 1Password, but it still targets developers and company infrastructure rather than personal password management.

products.name: Doppler
products.description: A polished cloud secrets manager built for developer workflows, strong on convenience and compliance posture but proprietary and centralized.

privacy.note: Doppler says its platform helps teams secure, sync and automate secrets across environments and infrastructure.

transparency.note: Doppler publishes a trust center and says it maintains SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001:2022 documentation.

openness.note: Doppler is a proprietary cloud-based secrets management platform rather than open-source/self-hostable infrastructure.

security.note: Doppler's security materials describe SOC 2 Type II compliance, external testing and data-tokenization practices.

accessibility.note: Doppler markets a developer-friendly SaaS experience and start-free path, but it is still a team infrastructure tool.

products.name: AWS Secrets Manager
products.description: Amazon's native cloud secrets manager, useful for AWS-heavy teams but inherently tied to the AWS identity, billing and infrastructure stack.

privacy.note: AWS Secrets Manager stores, retrieves and rotates database credentials, application credentials, OAuth tokens, API keys and other secrets.

transparency.note: AWS publishes extensive product and user-guide documentation for Secrets Manager behavior and rotation workflows.

openness.note: AWS Secrets Manager is a proprietary AWS managed service rather than open-source or self-hostable software.

security.note: AWS lists encryption, central auditing, access management, rotation and replication as Secrets Manager capabilities.

accessibility.note: Secrets Manager is convenient inside AWS, but it requires AWS account, IAM and cloud-service literacy.

products.name: Azure Key Vault
products.description: Microsoft Azure's native service for keys, secrets and certificates, strongest for Azure teams and weaker for openness or cloud independence.

privacy.note: Azure Key Vault stores keys, secrets and certificates used by Azure applications and users.

transparency.note: Microsoft publishes Key Vault docs covering concepts, authentication, logging, monitoring and secret operations.

openness.note: Azure Key Vault is a proprietary Microsoft Azure managed service rather than open-source/self-hostable software.

security.note: Microsoft says Key Vault encrypts secrets at rest using a hierarchy of encryption keys protected by FIPS-validated modules.

accessibility.note: Key Vault is well documented for Azure users, but real use requires Azure account, Entra/IAM and cloud-architecture knowledge.

products.name: Google Cloud Secret Manager
products.description: Google Cloud's native secrets store, useful for GCP projects and serverless apps but still a proprietary cloud-platform dependency.

privacy.note: Google Cloud Secret Manager stores and manages sensitive data such as API keys, usernames, passwords and certificates.

transparency.note: Google publishes product and documentation pages for Secret Manager concepts, access and secret versions.

openness.note: Google Cloud Secret Manager is a proprietary Google Cloud managed service rather than open-source/self-hostable software.

security.note: Secret Manager supports centralized storage, IAM permissions and secret versions for application credentials and configuration.

accessibility.note: Secret Manager is straightforward inside Google Cloud, but still assumes Google Cloud account and IAM knowledge.

products.name: Akeyless
products.description: A commercial enterprise secrets and access platform that consolidates secrets, just-in-time access and compliance controls across hybrid environments.

privacy.note: Akeyless describes secrets management around least privilege, zero trust, access control, just-in-time access and audit logs.

transparency.note: Akeyless publishes a trust center with security and compliance posture information.

openness.note: Akeyless is a proprietary commercial secrets-management platform rather than an open-source vault.

security.note: Akeyless emphasizes detailed audit logs, policy enforcement and reducing hardcoded-secret sprawl.

accessibility.note: Akeyless is built for enterprise secrets and compliance programs, so it is less accessible to individuals than consumer vaults.

products.name: CyberArk Privilege Cloud
products.description: A major enterprise privileged-access platform and useful floor comparison: very strong on access control, but admin-centered, proprietary and far from a personal vault.

privacy.note: CyberArk Privilege Cloud controls privileged access by storing privileged identities in safes and giving access only to authorized users.

transparency.note: CyberArk publishes product docs and PAM materials, but the platform is proprietary enterprise software.

openness.note: CyberArk Privilege Cloud is a proprietary privileged-access product rather than an open-source password or secrets manager.

security.note: CyberArk says its PAM solutions discover and manage privileged accounts and credentials, isolate sessions and remediate risky activity.

accessibility.note: The product is designed for enterprise administrators and security teams, not ordinary personal password management.

products.name: FEITIAN ePass FIDO
products.description: A hardware security-key family with FIDO2/WebAuthn options, useful when someone wants a YubiKey alternative for phishing-resistant MFA.

privacy.note: FEITIAN FIDO keys use WebAuthn-compatible hardware authentication rather than reusable shared passwords.

transparency.note: FEITIAN publishes product-family and individual ePass FIDO2-NFC specifications.

openness.note: The key follows FIDO/WebAuthn standards but is proprietary hardware and firmware.

security.note: FEITIAN says the ePass FIDO2-NFC key is FIDO U2F and FIDO2 certified and provides phishing-resistant authentication for online accounts.

accessibility.note: FEITIAN offers multiple form factors including USB, NFC, Lightning and biometric models, though setup still requires account-by-account registration.

products.name: Kensington VeriMark Guard
products.description: A biometric FIDO2 security key for people who want hardware-backed MFA plus fingerprint convenience instead of a simple touch-only key.

privacy.note: Kensington VeriMark Guard uses local fingerprint security-key authentication rather than a password shared with websites.

transparency.note: Kensington publishes specifications including supported operating systems, USB-C connection, FIDO/FIDO2 certification and warranty.

openness.note: VeriMark Guard supports FIDO2/WebAuthn and U2F standards, but the hardware and firmware are proprietary.

security.note: Kensington lists FIDO2, WebAuthn/CTAP2 and FIDO U2F support with biometric authentication.

accessibility.note: The fingerprint model can reduce repeated PIN friction, though it requires compatible devices and per-service setup.

products.name: Swissbit iShield Key
products.description: A European hardware-key line for teams that want FIDO2 plus enterprise-friendly options such as PIV, OTP and document-signing workflows.

privacy.note: Swissbit positions iShield keys as hardware authenticators for phishing-resistant passwordless access.

transparency.note: Swissbit publishes product pages, user manuals and press materials describing supported standards and models.

openness.note: The iShield Key supports FIDO2 and related standards but is proprietary hardware rather than open-source hardware.

security.note: Swissbit says iShield Key Pro supports FIDO2, PIV, HOTP and TOTP protocols, with USB-C and USB-A model options.

accessibility.note: The key supports broad FIDO2 services and multiple interfaces, but enterprise features make it less beginner-oriented than simple consumer keys.

products.name: Thetis FIDO2 Security Key
products.description: A lower-cost FIDO2/U2F hardware-key option, useful as a budget-access comparison against more established security-key brands.

privacy.note: Thetis describes its FIDO2 key as hardware passkey/passwordless login and U2F two-step authentication, reducing reusable-password exposure.

transparency.note: Thetis publishes product pages listing FIDO2, U2F and TOTP/HOTP app support, but less public assurance depth than larger security-key vendors.

openness.note: The Thetis key follows FIDO/U2F standards but is proprietary hardware and firmware.

security.note: Thetis says the key supports FIDO2, FIDO U2F, 2FA/MFA and passkey passwordless login for services such as Google, GitHub and Salesforce.

accessibility.note: Thetis markets the FIDO2 key as budget-friendly and easy to use, though hardware-key setup remains account-by-account.
